methodological_rigor.justification: This is a single-center retrospective comparison of robot-assisted versus open pancreatoduodenectomy (400 consecutive patients; 162 RPD, 238 OPD) with a clearly defined composite endpoint (textbook outcome, including absence of mortality, major complications, CR-POPF, PPH, bile leak, and readmission within 1 month). The authors attempt to address selection bias using propensity score matching (1:1 matching with caliper 0.20) and then evaluate predictors of TO with univariate/multivariate logistic regression reporting odds ratios and 95% CIs. Important limitations are inherent to the design and are acknowledged, including differing indications for RPD vs OPD (e.g., advanced tumors requiring vascular/other organ resection routed to OPD) and potential chronological and surgeon-training confounding.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: The evidence level is Oxford 2b because this is an individual (retrospective) cohort study comparing two surgical approaches with measured perioperative outcomes. The clinical relevance is high: after matching, RPD is associated with meaningfully better short-term outcomes including lower blood loss (75 vs 270 mL), shorter length of stay (13 vs 22 days), fewer major complications (17.1% vs 44.4%), markedly lower CR-POPF (2.6% vs 28.2%), and a higher TO rate (76.9% vs 52.1%). The manuscript also reports multivariable association between robotic surgery and TO (odds ratio 3.04, p < 0.001), directly informing quality-improvement and patient-counseling discussions in high-volume centers.

reporting_quality.justification: As an observational comparative effectiveness study, STROBE is the appropriate reporting standard, and the manuscript reports key elements including cohort definition, endpoints (Clavien-Dindo, ISGPS POPF), and a concrete propensity-score approach with matching variables and caliper. The Results section provides quantitative outcome rates and describes reasons for reoperation and readmission, and the Discussion explicitly lists major confounding risks (selection, chronological bias, trainee proportion imbalance). The normalized manuscript does not include a data/code availability statement for the underlying database or analysis scripts, so reproducibility is limited to the described methods.

novelty_literature.justification: The contribution is primarily an incremental extension of the RPD vs OPD literature by focusing on textbook outcome (a multidimensional quality metric) and evaluating robotic surgery as an independent predictor of TO in a defined institutional training context. The finding that RPD is associated with higher TO after matching is valuable but sits within an established comparative-outcomes space where multiple meta-analyses and multicenter studies exist. Novelty is therefore moderate, driven more by endpoint framing and the TAKUMI-7 setting than by a new concept or method.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is well organized with clear definitions (TO and complication grading systems) and a results narrative that reports concrete effect sizes and p-values. The limitations are presented candidly and specifically (e.g., nonsynchronized enrollment periods and higher trainee proportion in OPD), which improves interpretability. The abstract is quantitatively grounded and matches the main text outcomes.

key_strengths: Large consecutive single-center cohort (n = 400) with clinically meaningful, well-defined composite quality endpoint (textbook outcome) and standardized complication definitions.
Appropriate attempt to mitigate confounding using propensity score matching (117 vs 117 after matching) plus multivariable modeling with effect estimates (ORs, 95% CIs).
Substantial matched-cohort differences favoring RPD in several short-term outcomes (blood loss, length of stay, major complications, CR-POPF) culminating in higher TO achievement.
key_concerns: Residual confounding remains likely because surgical approach assignment is nonrandom and indications differ (e.g., advanced tumors requiring vascular/other organ resection routed to OPD).
Chronological bias is plausible because RPD starts later and institutional learning/selection may differ across eras even with standardized ERAS protocols.
Imbalance in surgeon experience (higher trainee proportion in OPD) is a major potential confounder for complication and TO differences.
No long-term oncologic or survival outcomes are assessed, limiting inference about downstream benefit beyond perioperative quality metrics.
chief_reviewer.rationale: The matched analyses and clearly defined quality endpoint make this a strong retrospective outcomes paper, but the nonrandomized design and several acknowledged confounders cap the tier. At a solid tier-3 surgical/oncology journal, the work is plausible with revisions that more directly address confounding (especially trainee and era effects) and clarify generalizability.
